newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban said taking two towns, face attack.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban said taking two towns, face attack.

text.p: Afghanistan's fundamentalist Islamic Taleban militia recaptured two strategic towns north of the capital Kabul in a major offensive on Tuesday, Taleban officials and a local news service reported.
But they continued to face shelling from opposition forces still occupying hills near the lost towns of Golbahar and Jabal os-Siraj, a Pakistan-based Afghan news service said.

A senior Taleban official said the purist militia had taken Golbahar, and the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) later said the forces loyal to opposition leader Ahmad Shah Masood had also lost the nearby Jabal os-Siraj.
Masood's forces had taken both towns from the Taleban in an offensive last week.

Taleban Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told reporters at Pul-i-Khumri town, in the northeastern province of Baghlan: "This morning the Taleban launched a very wide offensive on Golbahar, clearing the area.
"We have also captured the rear of Jabal os-Siraj and Masood's forces are now surrounded there."
AIP said it had reports of fighting still raging around a textile mill in Golbahar and that Jabal os-Siraj fell to the Taleban about midday.
But it said Masood's forces had retreated to the nearby hills and could strike again.

The Taleban captured 14 opposition soldiers and five of its own fighters were killed, AIP said. There was no immediate information about opposition casualties, it said. Taleban jets also pounded Golbahar earlier on Tuesday.
In a related development, a U.N. envoy seeking peace in Afghanistan was in Kabul on Tuesday, meeting the Taleban government officials, the official Kabul radio said.

The broadcast, monitored in Islamabad, said U.N. special envoy for Afghanistan Norbert Holl met deputy foreign minister Sher Mohammad Abbas Stanakzai and Communications Minister Mullah Mohammad Dad. It gave no details.
Masood, who is based in the Panjsher Valley, captured Jabal os-Siraj on Friday, cutting off a Taleban force now based in Pul-i-Khumri, north of the Hindu Kush mountain range.
Jabal os-Siraj, 70 km (44 miles) north of Kabul, sits at the foot of the strategic Salang Pass, a key artery connecting the Afghan capital with the north of the country.
Despite the apparent capture of Jabal os-Siraj, the Taleban would still need to force a way through several other opposition-held areas to resupply their comrades in Pul-i-Khumri.
Mutaqi denied reports that Basir Salangi, one of Masood's commanders in the Salang Pass, had rejoined his former chief after apparently defecting to the Taleban last week.
"Basir Salangi is still with the Taleban, but some of his men are with Masood," he said.
It was not clear if the territory Salangi controls, just north of Jabal os-Siraj, remained open to the Taleban.

The beleaguered Taleban in Pul-i-Khumri were consolidating on Tuesday after giving ground on Sunday and Monday. A Taleban commander at a frontline 35 km (22 miles) north of the town said an opposition attack had been beaten back.

"They launched an attack at 6 a.m. (0130 GMT) but we counter-attacked and pushed them back," Haji Ahmadullah told reporters who visited the area, where opposition forces were still shelling Taleban positions on Tuesday morning.

Taleban fighters said there had been no change in the southern frontline overnight, adding that opposition forces loyal to Syed Jafar Naderi still controlled the town of Doshi, 46 km (29 miles) south of Pul-i-Khumri.
Mutaqi said he was confident the Taleban could hold on to Pul-i-Khumri, despite their apparent isolation.

"We can't consider ourselves under siege because we control the whole of Baghlan province and we have sufficient supplies and stocks. Pul-i-Khumri is full of ammunition and we can stand against them for 10 years, God willing," he said.
"We now control the heart of the north and hope that our advances will spread to the whole of the north," he said.
He said 1,200 Taleban fighters who had been driven out of the northern opposition capital of Mazar-i-Sharif last week had joined their comrades in Pul-i-Khumri.

The Taleban, who took over the capital in September, have responded to the fall of Mazar-i-Sharif by sending thousands of new recruits to Kabul, mainly from Koranic schools in Pakistan and southern Afghanistan.
